title: Do Miracles Still Happen?
subtitle: Cessationist, continuationist, and open-but-cautious accounts of the miraculous in God's providence, and Hume's old objection.
triageNote: Whether God still works the extraordinary, healings, deliverances, undeniable answers to prayer, is a question about how God governs His world. It is not a boundary of the faith. Every view here confesses that God can do anything, that He worked real miracles in Scripture, and that He answers prayer. The argument is about whether the dramatic, sign-level miracle is normal in this age or rare and exceptional. That is a third-order matter. It runs between believers who pray for the sick at the same bedside and would each thank God if the sick rose. This page leaves aside the separate question of whether the gifts of tongues and prophecy continue. The Holy Spirit page takes that up. Here the question is the miraculous in providence itself. Hold loosely. Pray boldly either way.
question: A church gathers around a dying woman and prays for healing. Does anyone in the room expect God to actually do it. And what do they think happened if she lives, or if she dies. That is the question of this page. It is older and broader than any debate about spiritual gifts. Does God still pierce the ordinary course of nature with the extraordinary, the unmistakable sign, the healing medicine cannot explain, the deliverance that bends the laws He Himself set running. The Bible is full of such acts. But they cluster, around the Exodus, around the prophets, around Jesus and the apostles. And they run thin in the long stretches between. So is the age of obvious miracles essentially closed, a foundation laid once for all to authenticate revelation. Is it open and ongoing, the same Spirit doing the same works wherever faith and need meet Him. Or is the honest answer a watchful middle, God free to do the extraordinary, His people right to ask, and wise to weigh every claim soberly. And underneath it all sits the skeptic's old challenge. A miracle is by definition the least likely thing, and so never the most reasonable thing to believe.
whyItMatters:
This is the doctrine you are actually holding when you decide how to pray over someone who is dying. If you believe the age of miracles is essentially past, you will pray for grace and for the doctors and for a peaceful end. And you will mean it. You will not be crushed when the miracle does not come, because you never staked your faith on it. If you believe God still heals as freely as ever, you will pray with bold expectancy, you will lay on hands, you will ask for the impossible. And you will have to make sense of it when the impossible does not arrive. Both believers love the same dying woman. Their theology of miracles is the difference in how they kneel beside her.

Get it wrong in one direction and you can quietly stop expecting God to do anything at all. You reduce Him to a distant manager of natural processes, the deist's God in evangelical clothing. Prayer becomes a way of adjusting yourself rather than asking Him. Get it wrong in the other direction and you can manufacture miracles to keep the machine running. You blame the sick for their own unhealed bodies. You build a faith so dependent on signs that it collapses the first time the sign does not come. The historic positions are all trying to keep two things at once. God is free and able to do the extraordinary, and He has not promised to do it on demand. And ordinary providence, the slow faithfulness of daily bread and answered prayer, is itself the deeper miracle.

And it decides how you meet the skeptic, and the skeptic in your own chest at three in the morning. The challenge that miracles do not happen, cannot happen, are never rational to believe, is one of the oldest and most quoted in the modern world. The believer who has never thought it through will be ambushed by it. Know how the church has answered, and where the answers are strong and where they strain. That is part of being able to stand in a world that calls your deepest hope a superstition.

positions.name: Cessationism
positions.inOneLine: The dramatic, sign-level miracles served to authenticate God's appointed messengers and revelation. With that foundation laid in the apostles, such miracles have largely ceased, though God still answers prayer and may act extraordinarily as He wills.
positions.bestCase:
Let me first say what I am not claiming, because I am almost always heard as claiming more. I am not saying God cannot do miracles. He is God. He can part any sea He likes tomorrow morning. I am not saying He never does the extraordinary. I have prayed for the sick and seen recoveries I cannot explain, and I thank Him for them. What I am saying is narrower and, I think, more biblical. The era of dense, public, sign-level miracles, the kind that raised the dead on a street corner and authenticated a prophet, was tied to specific moments of revelation. And with the close of the apostolic foundation that era has largely passed. The Spirit did not leave. The circus left.

Look honestly at where the miracles cluster in Scripture, because this is the heart of my case. They do not run evenly across the centuries. They bunch at three hinge points: Moses and the Exodus, Elijah and Elisha, and Jesus and the apostles. Between those clusters are long stretches, centuries, where the people of God walked by faith with almost no public miracles at all. Why the clustering. Because the miracles authenticated new revelation. Paul calls them the signs of a true apostle. Hebrews says the great salvation was declared by the Lord and attested by God with signs and wonders, the verb in the past tense, a confirmation given when the message was first delivered. The function of the sign was to vouch for the messenger and the message. Once the message is delivered and the canon closed, the foundational signs have done their work, the way scaffolding comes down when the building stands.

This is not a cold doctrine, and I want you to feel why I hold it pastorally and not just exegetically. It protects the sufficiency of Scripture. When the dramatic sign is expected as normal, the hunger for fresh signs can quietly displace the finished word. People start chasing the next wonder instead of resting in the once-for-all wonder of the gospel. It protects the suffering. I have watched the sick told that their bodies stayed broken because their faith was too small. That cruelty is the natural fruit of a theology that expects healing on demand. And it protects honest eyes. A faith that must produce miracles to sustain itself will eventually start manufacturing them, and the watching world is right to distrust that. I would rather teach a believer to trust the God who is sovereign over her cancer whether He heals it or not than to teach her that her unhealed body is a verdict on her faith.

Where am I pressed hardest, and I will not flinch from it. My greatest difficulty is that the New Testament nowhere plainly says the miraculous will cease at the end of the apostolic age. The strongest text usually cited, that the perfect will come and the partial pass away in 1 Corinthians 13, most naturally refers to Christ's return, not the closing of the canon. I grant that. So my position rests more on the pattern of redemptive history and the function of signs than on a single proof-text that shuts the door. A thoughtful continuationist will press exactly there, asking by what verse I dare limit the Spirit. I answer that the burden runs the other way, that the clustering and the authenticating purpose are the Bible's own testimony to how miracles work. But I hold my view knowing it is an inference from the shape of Scripture rather than a flat command, and I hold it the more humbly for that.
advocates: much of the confessional Reformed tradition

positions.name: Continuationism
positions.inOneLine: The God who worked miracles in Scripture is unchanged, and the Spirit poured out at Pentecost is still poured out. So the same extraordinary works, healings, deliverances, signs, continue wherever faith meets need until Christ returns.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with the simplest argument, and I think the strongest. The God of the Bible does not have a former self. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost was poured out, Peter says, for you and your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to Himself, which is us. Nowhere does the New Testament announce an expiration date on the works of God. So the question I put to my cessationist brother is simple and, I think, hard for him to answer. By what authority do you tell the living God that the era of His extraordinary works is over. The default reading of the New Testament is that what God was doing through His people in Acts, He goes on doing. He is the same and His Spirit is the same and the need is the same.

Look at what Jesus actually said and did, and at what He told His followers to expect. He sent out the seventy to heal the sick and cast out demons, and they returned amazed. He said that whoever believes in Him will do the works that He does, and greater works than these. The Great Commission ends not with go and teach correct doctrine only, but with teaching them to observe all that I commanded you. And He had commanded healing and deliverance. And behold, I am with you always, the same powerful presence, to the end of the age. The book of Acts is not a description of a unique founding generation that pulls up the ladder behind it. It is the ordinary life of the church when the church actually believes the Spirit is present. The miracles thin out in church history not because God withdrew them but because the church's faith withdrew, settled, grew comfortable, and stopped asking.

And here is the fact that finally moves me more than any argument. It is happening. Across the global south, the church is poor and persecuted and has never been taught a theology that forbids the miraculous. And there the most careful researchers find healings, deliverances, and answered prayers on a scale the comfortable Western church has trained itself not to see. Men like Craig Keener, whose two-volume study Miracles documents case after case with names and medical detail. The Western believer who says miracles have ceased may simply be describing his own unbelieving neighborhood and mistaking it for the world. The Spirit did not stop. We stopped expecting, and you do not receive what you have decided in advance God will not give.

Let me be honest about my hardest ground, because the honest continuationist must be. The deepest problem is the prayer that goes unanswered, the faithful saint who is not healed, the deliverance that does not come. If the same Spirit does the same works, why is my godly friend still in the wheelchair after a thousand prayers. And how do I keep from the cruelty of telling her she lacks faith. I answer that healing is God's sovereign gift and not a vending machine. Even Paul left Trophimus sick and bore his own thorn the Lord refused to remove, so that expectancy and submission must be held together, bold to ask and ready to bow. But I grant that the gap between what I claim God still does and what I actually see Him do in any given hospital room is the place my view is pressed hardest. And I would rather live honestly in that gap, asking and sometimes not receiving, than close it by deciding in advance that God no longer acts.
advocates: Jack Deere (Surprised by the Power of the Spirit)

positions.name: The open-but-cautious view
positions.inOneLine: God is free to work miracles today and His people should pray for them with real expectancy, while weighing every claim soberly. The dramatic sign is the exception in this age rather than the rule, and ordinary providence is where God most often works.
positions.bestCase:
Let me stake out the ground I actually live on, because it is where I suspect most thoughtful Christians live once they stop having to defend a flag. I cannot say with the strict cessationist that the age of miracles is closed. I do not find that taught plainly anywhere in Scripture. And I have read the careful documentation, Keener's volumes and others, and watched things in answer to prayer that I will not explain away to keep a theory tidy. But I also cannot say with the enthusiastic continuationist that the dramatic miracle is simply normal Christian life. That is not what I see, not in the New Testament's own long quiet stretches and not in the church I actually pastor. So I hold the door open and I keep my eyes clear. Open, and cautious. The two words belong together.

Let me ground the open half first. The God of the Bible never resigned. There is no verse that retires Him, and the burden of proof falls heavily on anyone who would limit what the living God may do. So I pray for the sick expecting that God may heal, I lay on hands, I ask boldly. To do otherwise is a practical unbelief that has quietly emptied much of the Western church of any expectation that prayer changes anything. James says the prayer of faith will save the sick, and I take that as a standing invitation, not an expired one. The default posture of a believer should be expectancy, not resignation, and I repent of every prayer I have prayed without really believing God could answer it.

Now the cautious half, and it is just as biblical. Scripture itself sets miracles in the exceptional register, not the routine one. They cluster at the hinges of revelation and run thin between, the people of God spending most of their history walking by faith and not by sight. Paul, who raised the dead, also left Trophimus sick at Miletus and could not pray away his own thorn. He told Timothy to take a little wine for his frequent ailments rather than commanding a healing. So expectancy must be married to discernment. I weigh claims soberly. Scripture warns that signs and wonders can deceive and that the enemy counterfeits. And I have seen the damage when the sick are blamed for their own broken bodies and when manufactured wonders curdle into cynicism. And I hold fast to a truth both of my more confident brothers can underrate. The slow, faithful, unspectacular providence of God, the daily bread, the answered prayer no one filmed, the marriage healed over twenty years, is not a lesser thing than the dramatic sign. It may be the deeper miracle, and it is certainly the more common one.

Where am I pressed hardest, and I will own it. My view can look like a refusal to commit, a way of agreeing with everyone and risking nothing. It can look like holding the door open just enough to seem humble while never having to defend a single specific miracle. The cessationist says I have no principle, only a mood, and the continuationist says my caution is unbelief wearing the mask of wisdom. I feel both barbs. I answer that the New Testament itself models exactly this posture, bold prayer and sober discernment together, expectancy without entitlement. Holding two true things in tension is not cowardice but maturity. But I grant that my position is the hardest to state crisply and the easiest to live lazily. It asks of me the discipline to actually pray with expectancy and actually weigh with care, rather than using each half as an excuse to neglect the other.
advocates: many in the broad evangelical mainstream

biblicalEvidence.summary: This salvation was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and gifts of the Holy Spirit. The miracles are described as God's attesting witness to the message when it was first declared.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against continuationism, since the signs are tied to the founding attestation of the gospel and the verbs lean toward a completed witness.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Continuationism answers that God bearing witness by signs describes how the gospel is confirmed wherever it goes, not only at the start. Nothing in the verse says the witness has stopped. The open-but-cautious view reads it as showing the special density of confirming signs at the founding moment. That fits miracles being exceptional rather than routine, without retiring them.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works. Paul names signs and wonders as the marks that authenticated his apostolic office in particular.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against continuationism, since it ties a class of dramatic signs specifically to apostolic authentication, which by definition does not continue.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Continuationism answers that signs marked Paul as a true apostle against false ones. But the same chapter assumes miracles among ordinary believers elsewhere, so signs authenticated apostles without being limited to them. The open-but-cautious view reads it as evidence that the most concentrated, office-confirming signs were apostolic and exceptional, while leaving room for God's ongoing extraordinary works.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I do, and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father. Jesus extends His works to whoever believes, not to a single founding generation.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for cessationism, since the promise of doing Jesus' works is attached to belief itself, with no apparent time limit.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationism answers that the greater works are greater in scope, the worldwide spread of the gospel after Pentecost. Whoever believes is fulfilled representatively in the apostolic church, not a guarantee of sign-miracles to every believer in every age. The open-but-cautious view reads it as a real and continuing openness to God working through believers. It holds that alongside the New Testament's own evidence that such works were not uniformly distributed.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. The unchanging character of Christ is taken as the ground that the One who healed and delivered still heals and delivers, since He has no former self.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against cessationism, since it grounds expectation in the unchanging Christ and resists the idea that His ways with His people fundamentally shifted after the apostles.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationism answers that the verse affirms Christ's unchanging character and saving work, not a promise that the modes of His action never vary across redemptive history. God plainly worked differently in different eras while remaining the same God. The open-but-cautious view reads it as securing that God can and may still act extraordinarily, the open half of its position, without settling how often He does.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil, and the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick. A standing instruction to the ordinary church to pray for healing with expectancy.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against a strong cessationism, since it commands the gathered church, not only apostles, to pray for the sick expecting God to act.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationism affirms this fully as a command to pray for the sick. It notes that the verse promises God's sovereign answer through the prayer of faith, not a guaranteed sign-level healing on demand. So it coheres with God answering prayer without the apostolic gift of healing continuing. The continuationist reads it as proof that healing prayer is normal church life. The open-but-cautious view reads it as the very pattern it commends, bold prayer joined to submission to God's will.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul pleads three times for his thorn to be removed and is told My grace is sufficient for you. He leaves Trophimus sick at Miletus. Even in the apostolic age, with the gift of healing operative, healing was not automatic or universal.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against an over-confident continuationism that expects healing as the normal entitlement of faith, since the greatest apostle is left unhealed and leaves a friend sick.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Continuationism answers that these show healing is God's sovereign gift, not a guarantee, which it has always affirmed, and that exceptions do not prove cessation. The open-but-cautious view reads them as Scripture's own caution that the miraculous is exceptional even when present. They are the ground for marrying expectancy to discernment. Cessationism reads them as confirming that even in the founding era God's ordinary way was unhealed faithfulness.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The open-but-cautious view, a caution to all
biblicalEvidence.summary: False christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. The lawless one comes with all power and false signs and wonders. The Bible warns that the miraculous can deceive and be counterfeited.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: A standing caution to any view that treats a dramatic sign as automatic proof of God's hand, since Scripture itself says wonders can come from the deceiver.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All three views accept the warning. Cessationism takes it as further reason for sobriety about claimed miracles today. Continuationism reads it as a call to discern spirits, not to deny genuine miracles, since a counterfeit implies a real article. The open-but-cautious view treats it as the biblical charter for the cautious half of its name. It weighs every claim by its fruit and its fidelity to Christ rather than by its drama.

weighing:
My judgment, offered as one pastor reasoning beside you and not as a ruling you must adopt to share my pew. I hold this one loosely on purpose. I have watched both confident answers wound people, and the Bible itself seems less interested in settling the theory than in commanding the prayer.

I find myself standing on the open-but-cautious ground, and let me tell you the honest reason. When I read the New Testament looking for a verse that plainly closes the age of miracles, I do not find one. The strongest cessationist text, the perfect coming in 1 Corinthians 13, most naturally means Christ's return. And I cannot in conscience tell the living God His extraordinary works are over on the strength of an inference. So I will not say miracles have ceased. But when I read the same New Testament looking for the dramatic sign as the normal furniture of the Christian life, I do not find that either. I find Paul's thorn unremoved, Trophimus left sick, Timothy told to take wine for his stomach, and long biblical centuries of faith without public wonders. So I will not say the miracle is routine. The Bible itself holds expectancy and rarity together, and I want to hold them the way it does.

Let me say what the other two rooms have given me, because I have been fed in both. The cessationist has taught me to guard the sufficiency of Scripture and to refuse the cruelty that blames the sick for their own unhealed bodies. Warfield's worry about manufactured wonders was prophetic, because I have seen exactly the counterfeits he feared. The continuationist has rebuked my practical unbelief, and I deserve the rebuke. I have prayed too many limp prayers that did not really expect God to do anything. Keener's careful documentation has made me ashamed of how much I had decided in advance God would not do. I needed both corrections, and I think most of us do.

So I land here, tentatively. God is free and able to do the extraordinary, and His people are right to ask boldly and lay on hands and expect that He may. And the dramatic sign is the exception in this age and not the rule. The slow faithful providence of daily bread and answered prayer no one filmed may be the deeper miracle, and is certainly the more common one. I would rather pray with expectancy and bow with submission, holding both, than purchase a crisp theory by dropping one of them. And I have learned that the careful cessationist at the bedside and the bold continuationist at the same bedside are both praying to a God who can raise the dead. If she rises, all of us will fall on our faces and thank the same Lord.
charitableDisagreement:
It is easy to make this a contest of who honors God more. The cessationist accuses the continuationist of credulity and emotionalism and chasing signs. The continuationist accuses the cessationist of unbelief, of putting the Spirit in a box and quietly worshiping a God who no longer does anything. Both accusations land sometimes, which is exactly why both are unfair as a rule. Refuse them.

Hear what each is guarding. The cessationist is guarding the sufficiency of the finished word against a restless hunger for fresh wonders. He guards the suffering saint from the cruelty of being told her unhealed body is a verdict on her faith. The continuationist is guarding the church from a practical deism that has stopped expecting God to act at all. He guards the testimony of believers across the world who are seeing things the comfortable West has trained itself not to see. The open-but-cautious believer is guarding the conviction that you need not choose between bold prayer and sober discernment, that Scripture itself marries expectancy to caution. None of the three loves God less. Each is watching a wall the others have turned their back to.

So is this a hill to die on. No, and saying so plainly is itself an act of care. That God can do anything, that He worked real miracles in Scripture, and that He still answers prayer is held by all three and is near the heart of the faith. But whether the dramatic sign is normal or exceptional in this age is a third-order question. It is a matter of wisdom about how to read the pattern of Scripture and how to pray at a bedside. Faithful believers have answered it differently while kneeling side by side. Hold the power and freedom of God with your whole weight. Hold your theory of how often He bends nature with a much lighter hand. Do not question the faith of the believer who prays beside you with a different expectation. When the dying woman is in the room, the cessationist and the continuationist and the cautious believer all do the same thing. They pray, and they leave the answer where it has always belonged, in the hands of the God who is free.

relatedDebates.topic: The continuation of the spiritual gifts
relatedDebates.note: Distinct from the miraculous in providence is the question of whether the gifts of the Spirit, tongues, prophecy, healing as a gift, continue today. The Holy Spirit page takes that up on its own terms. The two questions overlap but are not the same. One can believe God still works miracles while remaining cautious about the gift of prophecy, or the reverse.

relatedDebates.topic: Providence and the laws of nature
relatedDebates.note: A miracle is usually defined against the ordinary course of nature God upholds. That means your doctrine of providence shapes your doctrine of miracles. If God concurs in every natural event, a miracle is not God breaking in from outside but God acting in an unusual mode. The providence page in this set works out that wider framework.

relatedDebates.topic: The problem of evil and unanswered prayer
relatedDebates.note: Every view of miracles must reckon with the prayer that goes unanswered and the healing that does not come. That presses directly on the problem of evil. Why God heals one and not another, and how to pray with both expectancy and submission, is the pastoral edge where this doctrine is most tested.

relatedDebates.topic: Faith, evidence, and the testimony of witnesses
relatedDebates.note: Whether miracle claims today can be credibly established turns on how much weight eyewitness testimony can bear, the very question Hume raised. Keener's project is largely an argument that the testimony is far stronger and more widespread than the skeptical tradition allows. That connects the theology of miracles to the philosophy of evidence.
